When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

While it’s true that societal expectations often place men in "fixer" roles, **no one should be forced into a role they’re uncomfortable with or unskilled in**, and no one should be denied the opportunity to learn basic self-sufficiency because of gender stereotypes. - **Your refusal to help isn’t the problem**—her **demand that you do it** (while dismissing her own ability to learn) is the issue. What if they refuse? What if she’s stranded in an unsafe area? - It’s a **double standard**: You’re expected to be the "fixer" (even if you’re not skilled), but she’s expected to be the "damsel" who can’t do anything. This is not a healthy dynamic. --- ### **2. The "Damsel in Distress" Trope** Calling her out on playing the "damsel in distress" role is **100% valid**. This trope is not only outdated but also **demeaning**—it implies that women are inherently incapable or weak, which is a harmful stereotype. However, **how you framed it** could have been more constructive: - Instead of saying *"you’re acting helpless on purpose,"* you could have said: *"I get that you’re overwhelmed, but I taught you how to do this. If her support system reinforces these gender roles, **she may not even realize how limiting these beliefs are**. This is a cultural issue that goes beyond just the two of you, but it’s still your responsibility to **not enable it** in your relationship. --- ### **3. Your Boundaries Are Valid, But So Is Her Learning** You’re right to set boundaries—you shouldn’t be expected to know everything about car maintenance, and you’ve already done more than enough (buying the gauge, showing her how to use it). **However, your refusal to help now isn’t the solution—your refusal to *teach* her is the problem.** Here’s how you could approach this: - **Offer to show her again, but make it clear it’s her responsibility to learn:** *"I’m not going to pump your tire anymore, but I’ll show you how to do it at the gas station if you’re willing to try. If you still don’t want to, then you’ll need to figure out another solution—maybe a mechanic can help you set up a reminder system or you can get a portable air compressor."* - **Encourage her to take ownership:** *"If you don’t learn this, you’re putting yourself in a position where you might get stranded. That’s not safe. Do you want to take the time to learn, or do you want to rely on others?"* - **Address the gender role comments:** *"I don’t care if my friends/family think it’s a ‘man’s job’ to fix things. I’m not here to be your mechanic, and I don’t want you to think you can’t handle this yourself. If you want to be independent, you’ll have to learn."* --- ### **4. The Larger Problem: Who’s Holding Whom Accountable?** This situation highlights a **power imbalance** in your relationship: - **You’re financially supporting her** (which is great, but also means she may feel less pressure to be self-sufficient). - **She’s relying on you (and strangers) for basic tasks** instead of learning. - **Her male friends/family are reinforcing outdated roles**, which may make her less likely to challenge these beliefs. **Ask yourself:** - Are you enabling her by not pushing her to learn? - Are you setting a precedent where she expects you to always "fix" things for her? - Is this part of a larger pattern where she doesn’t take responsibility for her own life? If the answer to any of these is "yes," then **your refusal to help is actually a form of emotional withdrawal**, which could lead to resentment down the line. Instead, you should **hold her accountable in a way that empowers her**, not punishes her. --- ### **5. What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Stop helping her with the tire.** - You’ve already shown her how to do it. If she still won’t learn, she’ll have to deal with the consequences (e.g., getting a flat tire and needing to call for help). 2. **Have a direct but kind conversation:** - *"I’m not going to pump your tire anymore because I don’t think it’s fair for me to keep doing it when you won’t learn. If you don’t want to do it yourself, then you’ll need to find another solution—like a mechanic or a portable air compressor. I’m not your personal mechanic, and I don’t want you to rely on me for this."* - If she gets defensive, stay firm but compassionate: *"I’m not saying this to be mean. I’m saying it because I care about you. If you get stranded because you don’t know how to pump a tire, that’s not okay. You need to take responsibility for your own car."* 3. **Encourage her to seek help from others (not just men):** - *"If you’re worried about doing it yourself, maybe you could ask a female friend or a mechanic to show you. There are plenty of women who know how to fix cars—you don’t have to rely on men for this."* 4. **Set a deadline:** - *"If you don’t learn how to do this by [date], then you’ll have to pay for a mechanic to come to your house to fix it. I’m not doing it anymore."* 5. **Prepare for pushback:** - If she doubles down on the "it’s a man’s job" narrative, you can say: *"That’s a really old-fashioned way of thinking. I don’t want to be the only one who can fix things in this relationship. If you want to be equal, you’ll have to learn these skills too."* --- ### **6. Why This Matters in the Long Term** - **Self-sufficiency is a sign of maturity**, not gender. If she never learns basic car maintenance, she’ll always be dependent on others—which is not a sustainable or empowering way to live. - **Gender roles are harmful when they limit people.** You’re not "less of a man" for not knowing how to fix cars, but she’s not "less of a woman" for learning. The goal should be **mutual respect and shared responsibility**, not rigid stereotypes. - **This could be a sign of deeper issues.** If she’s comfortable with these gender dynamics, she may also be comfortable with other imbalances (e.g., financial dependence, emotional labor). Addressing this now can prevent bigger problems later. --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/10 (Not Acceptable)** Your **refusal to help is the right move**, but **your approach could be more constructive**. The real issue isn’t that you’re not helping—it’s that **she’s not taking responsibility for her own car**. Your job is to: 1. **Stop enabling her dependency.** 2. **Push her to learn (without guilt-tripping her).** 3. **Hold her accountable for her actions.** If she still refuses to engage, that’s on her—and you can’t keep fixing her problems for her. But **how you communicate this matters**. A firm but kind approach will be more effective than passive resistance (which could lead to resentment).
